name: FIN13 Case 1
desc: Attack by FIN13 against a Latin American bank

acts.d: The attacker scanned the perimeter of the victim looking for vulnerable webservices.
Scanned the targeted web server again.
Exploited a vulnerability in the Oracle WebLogic server, and passed malicious content via POST requests to a web page called AsyncResponseServiceHttps, and executed commands
Uploaded and accessed a webshell
Attempted to recon the DMZ segment where the infected webserver was operating.
Uploaded a zip archive of tools for various OS via the webshell onto the compromised web server
Implanted a WSO PHP webshell on the Zabbix server.
Attacker dropped a BlueAgave Perl webshell, configured on port 65510
Viewed folders and modified permissions to the "/srv/www/htdocs/gif" folder.
Enumerated the environment by running "whoami."
Viewed the "/etc/shadow" file on the Zabbix server.

acts.n: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
acts.d: Attackers viewed contents in the /var/log/apache2/ folder and removed entries of the access logs
Attacker launched massive ping sweeps against private subnets.
PortHole used to verify the first 10,000 TCP ports of any machine that responded to the ping sweep
Transferred additional tools to the Zabbix from the WebLogic Server
Attacker moved laterally from the Zabbix server to the Oracle Identity Manager server (in the DMZ)
Attacker dumped the sysadmin account related to the IAM service
Attacker used SSH to access the Oracle IAM server administrative UI
Attacker dumped the IAM local database of accounts allowing them to find domain accounts
Sniffed credentials passed by the IAM service to the DMZ servers.

acts.n: Indicator Removal on Host: File Deletion
acts.d: Attacker deleted RawCap output files and the RawCap tool
Attacker copied pr64.zip to the Backweb server
Attacker used Kerberoasting technique to collect the ticket from system memory and crack offline to obtain credentials.
Attacker accessed the Backweb server using customasp local user account
Attacker created a service and initialized it with an obfuscated PowerShell payload
Decoded PowerShell payload results in a similar PowerShell HTTP Bindshell that listens on port 65512
Attacker left several files in "Windows\Temp" directory, such as the Java scanner
Scanned internal subnets looking for additional servers
Attacker attempted to access the RSA servers by leveraging service accounts previously stolen through executing dictionary-based access attempts
Attacker enumerated databases in the same network segment as the RSA servers
Attacker scanned for MS-SQL servers
Attacker moved several tools to the Backweb server
The attackers dumped the database containing the SecurID token serials with the corresponding end-user accounts
Attacker accessed the Backweb server again multiple times using RDP and the sqlservice and sqlinstall accounts
Attacker harvested token serials from the database and collected daily token transactions in clear text stored inside a service account folder, where the storage procedure was scripted
Attacker logged into the bank users' accounts
